claim: Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) confer resistance against harsh conditions, including antibiotics, in Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) confer resistance against harsh conditions, including antibiotics, in Gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the function of LPS in bacterial defense.

claim: The lipopolysaccharide transport (Lpt) complex consists of seven proteins (A-G).
source: The lipopolysaccharide transport (Lpt) complex, consisting of seven proteins (A-G), exports LPS across the cellular envelope.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of the Lpt complex.

claim: The Lpt complex exports LPS across the cellular envelope.
source: The lipopolysaccharide transport (Lpt) complex, consisting of seven proteins (A-G), exports LPS across the cellular envelope.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the Lpt complex.

claim: LptB2FG forms an ATP-binding cassette transporter that transfers LPS to LptC.
source: LptB2FG forms an ATP-binding cassette transporter that transfers LPS to LptC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of LptB2FG.

claim: The β-jellyroll domain of LptF stably interacts with the LptG and LptC β-jellyrolls in both the apo and vanadate-trapped states.
source: The β-jellyroll domain of LptF stably interacts with the LptG and LptC β-jellyrolls in both the apo and vanadate-trapped states.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR spectroscopy data presented in the manuscript (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: ATP binding at the cytoplasmic side is allosterically coupled to the selective opening of the periplasmic LptF β-jellyroll domain.
source: ATP binding at the cytoplasmic side is allosterically coupled to the selective opening of the periplasmic LptF β-jellyroll domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR spectroscopy data showing conformational changes in the LptF β-jellyroll domain upon ATP binding (Figure 5E-F).

claim: In LptB2FG, ATP binding closes the nucleotide binding domains, causing a collapse of the first lateral gate as observed in structures.
source: In LptB2FG, ATP binding closes the nucleotide binding domains, causing a collapse of the first lateral gate as observed in structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data (Figures 2-3) and comparison with structural data.

claim: The second lateral gate, which forms the putative entry site for LPS, exhibits a heterogeneous conformation.
source: However, the second lateral gate, which forms the putative entry site for LPS, exhibits a heterogeneous conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data showing broad distance distributions for the second lateral gate (Figure 4).

claim: LptC binding limits the flexibility of the second lateral gate to two conformations.
source: LptC binding limits the flexibility of this gate to two conformations, likely representing the helix of LptC as either released from or inserted into the transmembrane domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data comparing LptB2FG and LptB2FGC (Figure 6D-E).

claim: The outer membrane (OM) serves as an initial line of defence against antibiotics in Gram-negative bacteria.
source: The outer membrane (OM), a crucial component of Gram-negative bacteria, serves as an initial line of defence against antibiotics (Nikaido, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nikaido, 2003.

claim: LPS is a glycolipid consisting of lipid A, core oligosaccharides and an O-antigen.
source: LPS is a glycolipid consisting of lipid A, core oligosaccharides and an O-antigen (Whitfield and Trent, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Whitfield and Trent, 2014.

claim: The Lpt system plays a central role in the biogenesis of OM, contributing significantly to its impermeability and resilience against environmental stress and host defenses.
source: The LPS transport (Lpt) system plays a central role in the biogenesis of OM, contributing significantly to its impermeability and resilience against environmental stress and host defenses (Wu et al., 2006; Ruiz et al., 2008; Chng et al., 2010; Lundstedt et al., 2021; Sperandeo et al., 2019; Ho et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The pathways for LPS synthesis, transport and regulation offer potential targets for novel antibiotics.
source: The pathways for LPS synthesis, transport and regulation offers potential targets for novel antibiotics (Vetterli et al., 2018; Zampaloni et al., 2024; Pahil et al., 2024; Mandler et al., 2018; Martin-Loeches et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Lpt system orchestrates unidirectional translocation of LPS from the inner membrane (IM) to the OM.
source: Comprising of seven essential components LptA-G (Figure 1A), the system orchestrates unidirectional translocation of LPS from the inner membrane (IM) to the OM (Lundstedt et al., 2021; Törk et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The LptB2FG complex forms an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter in the IM.
source: The LptB2FG complex forms an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter in the IM (Ruiz et al., 2008; Narita and Tokuda, 2009; Sperandeo et al., 2007; Thomas and Tampé, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The LptB subunits constitute the nucleotide-binding domains (NBD) and interact in a head-to-tail manner to create two nucleotide binding sites.
source: The LptB subunits constitute the nucleotide-binding domains (NBD Wang et al., 2014) and interact in a head-to-tail manner to create two nucleotide binding sites (NBSs, for ATP or ADP).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: The F and G subunits together form the transmembrane domains (TMDs) to create the LPS binding pocket.
source: The F and G subunits together form the transmembrane domains (TMDs) to create the LPS binding pocket (Dong et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The pseudo twofold symmetry of the TMDs creates two lateral gates on either side of the TMDs.
source: The pseudo twofold symmetry of the TMDs creates two lateral gates on either side of the TMDs.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural knowledge of the TMDs.

claim: LptC connects LptF-LptG with LptA to transfer LPS through the trans-periplasmic bridge towards LptDE.
source: LptC connects LptF-LptG (Tang et al., 2019; Owens et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019) with LptA (Sherman et al., 2018) to transfer LPS through the trans-periplasmic bridge towards LptDE (Villa et al., 2013; Tran et al., 2010; Suits et al., 2008; Okuda et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: LptB2FG apo structures revealed open NBDs with bound LPS inside the TMDs.
source: Previously, LptB2FG apo structures revealed open NBDs with bound LPS inside the TMDs (Figure 1B–C; Tang et al., 2019; Owens et al., 2019; Luo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1B-C.

claim: Upon vanadate trapping, the NBDs dimerize causing a collapse of the LPS binding pocket, which has been suggested as a post-translocation state.
source: Upon vanadate trapping, the NBDs dimerize causing a collapse of the LPS binding pocket, which has been suggested as a post-translocation state (Figure 1D–E; Tang et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1D-E.

claim: Presence of LptC enlarged the cavity leading to a weaker interaction with LPS.
source: Presence of LptC enlarged the cavity leading to a weaker interaction with LPS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 A-B; Tang et al., 2019; Owens et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 A-B.

claim: In the LptB2FGC apo conformation, the transmembrane (TM) helix of LptC weakly interacts with LptG, but forms extensive hydrophobic interactions with TM5 of LptF.
source: In this conformation, the transmembrane (TM) helix of LptC weakly interacts with LptG, but forms extensive hydrophobic interactions with TM5 of LptF.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis of LptB2FGC.

claim: The periplasmic β-jellyroll domains of LptF and LptG are very flexible leading to a reduced resolution in structures.
source: The periplasmic β-jellyroll domains of LptF and LptG are very flexible leading to a reduced resolution.
evidence: This is an observation from structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: LptB2FGC structures in the AMP-PNP or vanadate-trapped state did not reveal the transmembrane helix of LptC (TM-LptC).
source: LptB2FGC structures in the AMP-PNP or vanadate-trapped state did not reveal the transmembrane helix of LptC (TM-LptC), thereby revealing a nearly identical conformation of NBDs and TMDs as with the LptB2FG structures (Tang et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tang et al., 2019 and Li et al., 2019.

claim: The β-jellyroll domains were barely resolved in LptB2FGC structures in the AMP-PNP or vanadate-trapped state.
source: Also, the β-jellyroll domains were barely resolved (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 C-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 C-D.

claim: It was proposed that upon ATP binding, TM-LptC moves away from the LptG-TM1 – LptF-TM5 interface, leading to a collapse of the binding pocket and expulsion of LPS to the β-jellyroll domain of LptF.
source: It was proposed that upon ATP binding, TM-LptC moves away from the LptG-TM1 – LptF-TM5 interface. This would lead to a collapse of the binding pocket and expulsion of LPS to the β-jellyroll domain of LptF.
evidence: This is a previously proposed mechanism cited from the literature.

claim: The NBDs displayed a mean interspin distance centred around 5 nm in micelles in the apo state when observed at position B_M134R1.
source: In agreement with the apo structure, the NBDs displayed a mean interspin distance centred around 5 nm in micelles when observed at position B_M134R1 (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: The NBD interspin distance decreased below 4 nm in the vanadate-trapped state.
source: This distance decreased below 4 nm in the vanadate-trapped state.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: With ATP, a mixed population was observed with the major peak corresponding to the closed conformation of the NBDs.
source: With ATP a mixed population was observed with the major peak corresponding to the closed conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mg2+ ions are not necessary for the closure of the NBDs.
source: Thus, Mg2+ ions are not necessary for the closure of the NBDs.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that ATP-EDTA (without Mg2+) causes NBD closure.

claim: With ADP-Mg2+ the NBDs do not close, though the overall flexibility is somewhat increased.
source: With ADP-Mg2+ the NBDs do not close, though the overall flexibility is somewhat increased (as gauged from the width of the distribution).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In proteoliposomes, the NBDs in the apo-state revealed a similar mean distance to micelles, yet with a larger width suggesting an increased dynamics.
source: Overall, the data in the apo-state revealed a similar mean distance, yet with a larger width suggesting an increased dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data in proteoliposomes shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Vanadate-trapping closed the NBDs in proteoliposomes as well.
source: As observed in micelles, vanadate-trapping closed the NBDs in PLS as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data in proteoliposomes shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: The nucleotide-induced closure of NBDs as observed in micelles and structures is maintained in the native-like lipid bilayers.
source: Overall, the nucleotide-induced closure as observed in micelles (and the structures) is maintained in the native-like lipid bilayers for the NBDs.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing PELDOR data in micelles and proteoliposomes.

claim: For the apo-state in micelles, the distances for the lateral gate-1 are similar to the corresponding simulation on the LPS-bound structure.
source: For the apo-state in micelles, the distances for the lateral gate-1 are similar to the corresponding simulation on the LPS-bound structure (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data and simulations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Vanadate-trapping resulted in an increase of the distances at lateral gate-1 in agreement with the simulation.
source: Vanadate-trapping resulted in an increase of the distances in agreement with the simulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The increased distance at lateral gate-1 upon vanadate-trapping results from a coordinated movement of LptF-TM1 towards the cavity accompanied with an outward shift of LptG-TM5.
source: Though the central cavity collapses, this increased distance results from a coordinated movement of LptF-TM1 towards the cavity accompanied with an outward shift of LptG-TM5 (Figure 3E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from structural analysis and PELDOR data.

claim: Addition of ATP resulted in an equilibrium between the two conformations at lateral gate-1.
source: Addition of ATP resulted in an equilibrium between the two conformations.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The PELDOR data validate a LPS binding competent conformation in the apo- and ADP-Mg2+ states accompanied with a collapse of the gate in the ATP and vanadate-trapped post-hydrolytic state.
source: Altogether, the PELDOR data validate a LPS binding competent conformation in the apo- and ADP-Mg2+ states accompanied with a collapse of the gate in the ATP and vanadate-trapped post-hydrolytic state.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the PELDOR data on lateral gate-1.

claim: For the apo state in proteoliposomes, lateral gate-1 exhibited a broader distribution spanning the range corresponding to both structures.
source: Interestingly, for the apo state in PLS, this gate exhibited a broader distribution spanning the range corresponding to both structures (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data in proteoliposomes shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: In the vanadate-trapped state in proteoliposomes, the overall distribution of lateral gate-1 got narrowed but the overall spread remained similar, suggesting a more flexible conformation of this gate in PLS.
source: In the vanadate-trapped state the overall distribution got narrowed (the minor peak at a longer distance is not interpreted due to a larger uncertainty). However, the overall spread of the distribution remained similar, suggesting a more flexible conformation of this gate in PLS, which is minimally affected by ATP binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data in proteoliposomes shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: The lateral gate-2 between LptG-TM1 – LptF-TM5 revealed a more dynamic behavior in micelles.
source: Interestingly, the lateral gate-2 between LptG-TM1 – LptF-TM5 revealed a more dynamic behavior in micelles (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: In the apo state, lateral gate-2 has a broad conformational distribution spanning the LPS bound (open) and vanadate-trapped (closed) structures.
source: In the apo state, it has a broad conformational distribution spanning the LPS bound (open) and vanadate-trapped (closed) structures (corresponding simulations are shown in orange lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the vanadate-trapped and ATP samples, the major population of lateral gate-2 is centred at 2 nm (which is closer to the simulation on the vanadate-trapped structure).
source: In the vanadate-trapped and ATP samples, the major population is centred at 2 nm (which is closer to the simulation on the vanadate-trapped structure).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The decreased interspin distances at lateral gate-2 arise from a collapse of the cavity upon vanadate-trapping.
source: The decreased interspin distances arise from a collapse of the cavity upon vanadate-trapping (Figure 4E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from structural analysis and PELDOR data.

claim: ADP-Mg2+ gave a broad distribution at lateral gate-2 comparable to the apo-state.
source: ADP-Mg2+ also gave a broad distribution comparable to the apo-state.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the apo-state, lateral gate-2 appears to exist in an equilibrium between the two conformations as observed from the corresponding structures.
source: Thus, in the apo-state this gate appears to exist in an equilibrium between the two conformations as observed from the corresponding structures.
evidence: This is an inference from the PELDOR data showing broad distributions.

claim: ATP binding or vanadate-trapping shifts the equilibrium of lateral gate-2 towards the collapsed conformation.
source: ATP binding or vanadate-trapping shifts the equilibrium towards the collapsed conformation.
evidence: This is an inference from the PELDOR data.

claim: In proteoliposomes, the apo state of lateral gate-2 revealed a broad distribution validating the heterogeneity in the membrane environment.
source: In PLS as well, the apo state revealed a broad distribution validating the heterogeneity in the membrane environment (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data in proteoliposomes shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Vanadate-trapping somewhat narrowed the distribution of lateral gate-2 in proteoliposomes with only a fraction of the distances overlaying with the simulation for the corresponding structure.
source: Vanadate-trapping somewhat narrowed the distribution with (only) a fraction of the distances overlaying with the simulation for the corresponding structure (and with a more pronounced heterogeneity as compared with the micellar sample, Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data in proteoliposomes shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: The observed heterogeneity at lateral gate-2 is distinctly modulated upon LptC binding.
source: Further, the observed heterogeneity is distinctly modulated upon LptC binding (Figure 6D–E), suggesting that the internal flexibility around the labeled sites might have the least contribution to the broad distribution we experimentally observed.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing PELDOR data of LptB2FG and LptB2FGC.

claim: The room temperature continuous wave ESR spectra revealed the least flexibility for the lateral gate-2 spin pair.
source: Confirming these observations, the room temperature continuous wave ESR spectra revealed the least flexibility for this spin pair (Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by continuous wave ESR data.

claim: The structures captured two of the states from the broad conformational space of lateral gate-2.
source: Comparing this heterogeneity from the PELDOR data (Figure 4) with the corresponding simulations (in orange, Figure 4A–B), it appears that the structures captured two of the states from the broad conformational space.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing PELDOR data with structural simulations.

claim: Lateral gate-2 is suggested to be the entry point for LPS.
source: This gate is suggested to be the entry point for LPS (Owens et al., 2019) and the enhanced dynamics we observed might be required for efficient interaction with LPS and LptC (please see later sections).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Owens et al., 2019.

claim: The enhanced dynamics of lateral gate-2 might be required for efficient interaction with LPS and LptC.
source: This gate is suggested to be the entry point for LPS (Owens et al., 2019) and the enhanced dynamics we observed might be required for efficient interaction with LPS and LptC (please see later sections).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed dynamics.

claim: LptG-TM1 and LptF-TM5 helices interact rather weak in the structures, in particular in the LPS-bound state.
source: Supporting these observations, LptG-TM1 and LptF-TM5 helices interact rather weak in the structures, in particular in the LPS-bound state (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from structural analysis.

claim: Distances between positions F_S186R1 and G_V209R1 located on the β-jellyroll domains revealed a major peak in agreement with simulation on the LPS-bound structure.
source: Distances between positions F_S186R1 and G_V209R1 located on these domains revealed a major peak in agreement with simulation on the LPS-bound structure (Figure 5A–B) and a previous study (Cina and Klug, 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 5A-B and a citation.

claim: The overall spread of the distance distribution between LptF and LptG β-jellyroll domains remained rather similar in the vanadate-trapped state revealing a stable interaction.
source: The overall spread of the distribution remained rather similar in the vanadate-trapped state revealing a stable interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The LptF β-jellyroll in the apo-state showed a broad distribution, but with a major population staying in the closed conformation as observed in the structure.
source: The LptF β-jellyroll in the apo-state showed a broad distribution, but with a major population staying in the closed conformation as observed in the structure (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: In the vanadate-trapped state, the overall distribution of LptF β-jellyroll shifted towards longer distances revealing an opening of the LPS entry gate.
source: Interestingly, in the vanadate-trapped state, the overall distribution shifted towards longer distances revealing an opening of the LPS entry gate.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: There is a long-range allosteric coupling between nucleotide binding at the NBDs in the cytoplasm and opening of the LPS entry gate of LptF β-jellyroll in the periplasm.
source: Altogether, these observations reveal a long-range allosteric coupling between nucleotide binding at the NBDs in the cytoplasm and opening of the LPS entry gate of LptF β-jellyroll in the periplasm.
evidence: This is an inference from the PELDOR data showing coordinated conformational changes.

claim: The tight allosteric coupling may prime the LptF β-jellyroll domain to receive LPS once it is released from the cavity inside the TMDs.
source: Such a tight coupling might prime this domain to receive LPS once it is released from the cavity inside the TMDs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed allosteric coupling.

claim: The β-jellyroll domain of LptG revealed a considerably enhanced flexibility independent of ATP.
source: A strikingly different response was observed for the β-jellyroll domain of LptG. The equivalent spin pairs G_V209R1 – G_L234R1 and G_L152R1 – V209R1 revealed a considerably enhanced flexibility independent of ATP (Figure 5D and G–H) and revealing no such allosteric coupling with the NBDs.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 5D and G-H.

claim: The β-jellyroll domain of LptG revealed no allosteric coupling with the NBDs.
source: A strikingly different response was observed for the β-jellyroll domain of LptG. The equivalent spin pairs G_V209R1 – G_L234R1 and G_L152R1 – V209R1 revealed a considerably enhanced flexibility independent of ATP (Figure 5D and G–H) and revealing no such allosteric coupling with the NBDs.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 5D and G-H.

claim: Measurements between the β-jellyroll domains of LptF and LptC revealed a narrow distance distribution and hence a stable interaction between them in both apo and vanadate-trapped states.
source: Measurements between the β-jellyroll domains of LptF and LptC (F_L219R1 – C_T104R1) revealed a narrow distance distribution and hence a stable interaction between them in both apo and vanadate-trapped states (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: At the lateral gate-1 in LptB2FGC, the distance in the apo state is similar to the simulation on the structure.
source: At the lateral gate-1 (F_A45R1 – G_I335R1, Figure 6F and G–H), the distance in the apo state is similar to the simulation on the structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 6G-H.

claim: In the vanadate trapped state of LptB2FGC, the spread of the distance distribution at lateral gate-1 is increased, spanning the range of the simulations corresponding to both apo and vanadate-trapped structures.
source: In the vanadate trapped state, the spread of the distance distribution is increased, spanning the range of the simulations corresponding to both apo and vanadate-trapped structures (in the latter structure, TM-LptC is absent at the gate leading to a collapse of the cavity and an identical conformation with LptB2FG, though the distances increase due to an outward movement of LptG-TM5, see Figure 3B and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 6G-H.

claim: Distances corresponding to the apo state are present in the vanadate-trapped LptB2FGC sample possibly due to an incomplete vanadate-trapping or an equilibrium between the two conformations.
source: Distances corresponding to the apo state are present possibly due to an incomplete vanadate-trapping (or an equilibrium between the two conformations, which is rather unlikely) for this sample.
evidence: This is an inference from the PELDOR data.

claim: The results support TM-LptC dissociation in the vanadate-trapped state as observed in the structure.
source: Overall, the results support TM-LptC dissociation in the vanadate-trapped state as observed in the structure.
evidence: This is an inference from the PELDOR data on LptB2FGC.

claim: LptC binding reduced the overall flexibility of lateral gate-2 into two defined distance peaks as compared to LptB2FG alone.
source: LptC binding reduced the overall flexibility of this gate into two defined distance peaks as compared to LptB2FG alone (Figure 4A vs. Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing PELDOR data in Figure 4A and Figure 6D.

claim: LptC binding increases the separation between the helices forming lateral gate-2.
source: LptC binding is shown to increase the separation between these helices (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from structural analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The major distance peak at lateral gate-2 in LptB2FGC (centred around 2 nm) likely represents a conformation in which TM-LptC is released.
source: The major distance peak (centred around 2 nm) is shorter than the simulation on the LptB2FG apo structure (in magenta, Figure 6D, top panel), which therefore likely represents a conformation in which TM-LptC is released.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing PELDOR data with structural simulations.

claim: The second peak at lateral gate-2 in LptB2FGC corresponds to a larger separation between these helices, possibly representing the structure having the TM-LptC inserted at the gate.
source: The second peak corresponds to a larger separation between these helices, possibly representing the structure having the TM-LptC inserted at the gate (as position L325 is not resolved in the E. coli structure, corresponding simulation is not presented).
evidence: This is an inference from the PELDOR data.

claim: The first conformation (TM-LptC released) appears to be more favored under the experimental conditions.
source: The first conformation appears to be more favored under the experimental conditions.
evidence: This is an inference from the relative peak intensities in the PELDOR data.

claim: In the vanadate-trapped state of LptB2FGC, the second peak at lateral gate-2 disappeared and the overall distribution centred towards the TM-LptC released (LptB2FG) conformation.
source: In the vanadate-trapped state, the second peak disappeared and the overall distribution centred towards the TM-LptC released (LptB2FG) conformation (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The disappearance of the second peak in vanadate-trapped LptB2FGC is in line with the lack of density for TM-LptC in the vanadate-trapped LptB2FGC structure.
source: This is in line with the lack of density for TM-LptC in the vanadate-trapped LptB2FGC structure.
evidence: This is an inference connecting PELDOR data with structural observations.

claim: The experimental distribution at lateral gate-2 in vanadate-trapped LptB2FGC is longer than the corresponding simulation, suggesting a somewhat farther separation between these helices.
source: The experimental distribution is longer than the corresponding simulation (orange line in Figure 6E), suggesting a somewhat farther separation between these helices.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing PELDOR data with simulations.

claim: In the apo and vanadate-trapped states, the majority of the observed complex peaks represent LPS bound to LptB2FG.
source: In the apo and vanadate-trapped states, the majority of the observed complex peaks represent LPS bound to LptB2FG, while some LPS-free LptB2FG can as well be seen (indicated in grey and red shades, respectively for both 1- and 2- charge states).
evidence: This claim is supported by LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 6I-K.

claim: LPS is co-purified with LptB2FG in micelles.
source: Thus, LPS is co-purified with LptB2FG in micelles.
evidence: This is an inference from the LILBID-MS data.

claim: Presence of LPS-bound LptB2FG in the vanadate-trapped state is not unexpected as the PELDOR data revealed a heterogenous conformation for the LPS entry gate other than the collapsed conformation.
source: Presence of LPS-bound LptB2FG in the vanadate-trapped state is not unexpected as the PELDOR data revealed a heterogenous conformation for the LPS entry gate other than the collapsed conformation (Figure 4B and G).
evidence: This is an inference connecting LILBID-MS and PELDOR data.

claim: Under the hydrolysing conditions, LPS is completely released from LptB2FG.
source: However, under the hydrolysing conditions, LPS is completely released from LptB2FG.
evidence: This claim is supported by LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 6K.

claim: LptB2FG and LptB2FGC structures revealed a similar structure in the vanadate-trapped state leaving no trace for TM-LptC and the β-jellyroll domains were not resolved.
source: LptB2FG and LptB2FGC structures revealed a similar structure in the vanadate-trapped state leaving no trace for TM-LptC and the β-jellyroll domains were not resolved (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an observation from structural analysis.

claim: Available structures possess either AMP-PNP or ADP-VO43- as nucleotides (both in a closed conformation of the TMDs and NBDs).
source: Available structures possess either AMP-PNP or ADP-VO43- as nucleotides (both in a closed conformation of the TMDs and NBDs), thereby limiting details on how ATP binding and hydrolysis are coupled to the conformational changes and LPS transport.
evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of available structural data.

claim: For the NBDs and the two lateral gates of LptB2FG, PELDOR data validated the conformational changes in micelles as observed from the structures.
source: For the NBDs and the two lateral gates of LptB2FG, PELDOR data validated the conformational changes in micelles as observed from the structures.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the PELDOR results.

claim: Upon ATP binding and/or vanadate-trapping, the NBDs and the two lateral gates moved in a coordinated manner to collapse the LPS binding pocket.
source: Upon ATP binding and/or vanadate-trapping, the NBDs and the two lateral gates moved in a coordinated manner to collapse the LPS binding pocket (Figures 2—4).
evidence: This is a summary inference from the PELDOR data shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: The minimal interaction between the corresponding helices in the LptB2FG structures suggest that the flexibility is inbuilt and might have an important role for the function.
source: The minimal interaction between the corresponding helices (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) in the LptB2FG structures suggest that the flexibility is inbuilt and might have an important role for the function.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural observations.

claim: The PLS environment modulates the observed conformation in LptB2FG.
source: The PLS environment modulates the observed conformation in LptB2FG.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing PELDOR data in micelles and proteoliposomes.

claim: The lateral gate-1 has a broader distribution in PLS, which is minimally affected by vanadate-trapping.
source: The lateral gate-1 has a broader distribution in PLS, which is minimally affected by vanadate-trapping (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data in proteoliposomes.

claim: The heterogeneity for the lateral gate-2 is more pronounced in PLS.
source: Also, the heterogeneity for the lateral gate-2 is more pronounced in PLS.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data in proteoliposomes.

claim: The liposomes are made from E. coli polar lipid extract.
source: The liposomes are made from E. coli polar lipid extract.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental methods.

claim: In the polar lipid extract, phosphatidylethanolamine is the predominant lipid component with minor amounts of phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin.
source: In the polar lipid extract, phosphatidylethanolamine is the predominant lipid component with minor amounts of phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli polar lipid extract composition.

claim: The differences in the heterogeneity observed in proteoliposomes might not be due to the presence of LPS.
source: Thus, the differences in the heterogeneity we observed in proteoliposomes might not be due to the presence of LPS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lipid composition.

claim: The observations in PLS are qualitatively similar to the micellar sample.
source: Overall, the observations in PLS are qualitatively similar to the micellar sample (also see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 for the continuous wave (cw) ESR spectra) and further experiments are required to clarify how the membrane would influence LptB2FGC conformation.
evidence: This is a summary statement comparing results in different environments.

claim: In LptB2FG, the two β-jellyroll domains stably interact in the apo and vanadate-trapped conditions.
source: In LptB2FG, the two β-jellyroll domains stably interact in the apo and vanadate-trapped conditions (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Binding of nucleotides is allosterically coupled to a selective opening of LptF β-jellyroll with little effect on the LptG β-jellyroll.
source: Interestingly, binding of nucleotides is allosterically coupled to a selective opening of LptF β-jellyroll with little effect on the LptG β-jellyroll (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: The gate opening of LptF β-jellyroll was shown to be essential for cell growth.
source: This opening was shown to be essential for cell growth and it was suggested that movement of LPS, but not ATP binding or hydrolysis pushes the gate open (Owens et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Owens et al., 2019.

claim: It was suggested that movement of LPS, but not ATP binding or hydrolysis pushes the LptF β-jellyroll gate open.
source: This opening was shown to be essential for cell growth and it was suggested that movement of LPS, but not ATP binding or hydrolysis pushes the gate open (Owens et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a previously proposed mechanism cited from Owens et al., 2019.

claim: The results confirm that the gate opening of LptF β-jellyroll is allosterically regulated through ATP binding and/or hydrolysis.
source: However, our results confirm that the gate opening is allosterically regulated through ATP binding and/or hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the PELDOR data showing ATP-dependent conformational changes.

claim: The LptF β-jellyroll starts from TM3 and ends on TM4.
source: This β-jellyroll start from TM3 and ends on TM4.
evidence: This is structural knowledge about the LptF β-jellyroll domain.

claim: TM3 is connected to the coupling helix and TM4 is connected to the cytoplasmic loop-2, which harbours the conserved R292 directly interacting with the nucleotide.
source: TM3 is connected to the coupling helix and TM4 is connected to the cytoplasmic loop-2, which harbours the conserved R292 directly interacting with the nucleotide (Tang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is structural knowledge supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2019.

claim: It is likely that one or both of the coupling helix and cytoplasmic loop-2 motifs are involved in the allosteric communication.
source: It is likely that one or both of these motifs are involved in the allosteric communication.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural connectivity.

claim: The LptG β-jellyroll domain exhibits significant internal flexibility.
source: Notably, the LptG β-jellyroll domain exhibits significant internal flexibility (Figure 5G-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: Biochemical studies showed that conserved residues in the LptG β-jellyroll domain are essential for cell growth.
source: Biochemical studies showed that conserved residues in this domain are essential for cell growth (Tang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2019.

claim: There is little evidence for a direct role of the LptG β-jellyroll domain in LPS binding.
source: Although there is little evidence for a direct role of this domain in LPS binding, the observed dynamics might be important for efficient transport.
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of evidence for a specific function.

claim: The observed dynamics of the LptG β-jellyroll domain might be important for efficient transport.
source: Although there is little evidence for a direct role of this domain in LPS binding, the observed dynamics might be important for efficient transport.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed dynamics.

claim: In LptB2FG-C, the β-jellyrolls of LptC and LptF interact both in both apo and vanadate-trapped states.
source: Similarly, in LptB2FG-C, the β-jellyrolls of LptC and LptF interact both in both apo and vanadate-trapped states (Figure 6A–C), which altogether might form a continuous pathway for LPS transfer towards LptA.
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: The β-jellyrolls of LptC and LptF might form a continuous pathway for LPS transfer towards LptA.
source: Similarly, in LptB2FG-C, the β-jellyrolls of LptC and LptF interact both in both apo and vanadate-trapped states (Figure 6A–C), which altogether might form a continuous pathway for LPS transfer towards LptA.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the stable interaction observed.

claim: The β-jellyrolls were not fully resolved in the vanadate-trapped structure of LptB2FG and LptB2FGC, revealing a considerable flexibility.
source: The β-jellyrolls were not fully resolved in the vanadate-trapped structure of LptB2FG (Figure 1) and LptB2FGC (Li et al., 2019), revealing a considerable flexibility.
evidence: This is an observation from structural studies.

claim: The exact role for the enhanced dynamics of β-jellyrolls is unclear and it may somehow facilitate LPS release.
source: The exact role for this enhanced dynamics is unclear and it may somehow facilitate LPS release.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of observed dynamics.

claim: The narrow distance distributions observed for β-jellyrolls reveal that these domains might move as rigid bodies while sampling a broad conformational space.
source: The narrow distance distributions we observed reveal that these domains might move as rigid bodies while sampling a broad conformational space.
evidence: This is an inference from the PELDOR data.

claim: LPS is released upon ATP hydrolysis by LptB2FG.
source: The LILBID-MS data show that LPS is released upon ATP hydrolysis by LptB2FG (Figure 6I–K, Figure 7 steps 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by LILBID-MS data shown in Figure 6I-K.

claim: LptC is required for a productive transport cycle in the wild-type protein.
source: Thus, LptC is required for a productive transport cycle in the wild-type protein (Sherman et al., 2018; Falchi et al., 2023; Wilson and Ruiz, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The TM-LptC dynamically associates and dissociates at the lateral gate-2, even in the apo-state while its β-jellyroll domain is firmly bound to LptF β-jellyroll.
source: Our observations suggest that the TM-LptC dynamically associates and dissociates at the lateral gate-2, even in the apo-state while its β-jellyroll domain is firmly bound to LptF β-jellyroll (Figure 7, step 3).
evidence: This is an inference from the PELDOR data on LptB2FGC.

claim: Such a dynamic behavior of TM-LptC has previously been suggested based on the Klebsiella pneumoniae LptB2FGC structure, which showed density for the short N-terminus segment of TM-LptC.
source: Such a dynamic behavior of TM-LptC has previously been suggested based on the Klebsiella pneumoniae LptB2FGC structure, which showed density for the short N-terminus segment of TM-LptC (Luo et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Luo et al., 2021.

claim: Vanadate trapping induces the TM-LptC released conformation of the lateral gates.
source: Vanadate trapping induces the TM-LptC released conformation of the lateral gates (Figure 6D–E and G–H), in agreement with the structures, which also leads to LPS release (Tang et al., 2019; Owens et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by PELDOR data and citations.

claim: ATP binding/hydrolysis might be coupled to the collapse of the TMDs and expulsion of LPS.
source: Thus, ATP binding/hydrolysis might be coupled to the collapse of the TMDs and expulsion of LPS.
evidence: This is an inference from the PELDOR and LILBID-MS data.

claim: ATP binding might allosterically open the LptF β-jellyroll.
source: Inferring from our observations on LptB2FG (Figure 5), ATP binding might allosterically open the LptF β-jellyroll (Figure 7, step 4), which might subsequently close after passing LPS to the LptC β-jellyroll to prevent any backflow (Tang et al., 2019; Figure 7, step 5).
evidence: This is an inference from the PELDOR data on LptB2FG.

claim: The LptF β-jellyroll might subsequently close after passing LPS to the LptC β-jellyroll to prevent any backflow.
source: Inferring from our observations on LptB2FG (Figure 5), ATP binding might allosterically open the LptF β-jellyroll (Figure 7, step 4), which might subsequently close after passing LPS to the LptC β-jellyroll to prevent any backflow (Tang et al., 2019; Figure 7, step 5).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed dynamics and cited literature.

claim: Through repeating this cycle, LptB2FG might push LPS along the trans-periplasmic bridge in a unidirectional manner according to the Pez candy dispenser model.
source: Through repeating this cycle, LptB2FG might push LPS along the trans-periplasmic bridge in a unidirectional manner according to the Pez candy dispenser model (Okuda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed mechanism and a citation to the Pez model.

claim: LptB2FG belongs to the type VI class of ABC transporter.
source: LptB2FG belongs to the type VI class of ABC transporter.
evidence: This is a classification statement based on established knowledge.

claim: All the cysteine variants could be labeled with high efficiency.
source: All the cysteine variants could be labeled with high efficiency (Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: All the variants actively hydrolysed ATP.
source: All the variants actively hydrolysed ATP, in line with the conformational changes observed from PELDOR/DEER experiments following vanadate-trapping (Figures 2—6).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATPase activity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The functionality of the spin labeled variants is in line with the conformational changes observed from PELDOR/DEER experiments following vanadate-trapping.
source: All the variants actively hydrolysed ATP, in line with the conformational changes observed from PELDOR/DEER experiments following vanadate-trapping (Figures 2—6).
evidence: This is an inference connecting ATPase activity with PELDOR observations.
